title: What pattern do the four angles at a crossing show?
description: Two lines cross and the four angles are written round the crossing as measured. The board adds each pair of neighbours and compares each angle with the one facing it, then Keeko doubts that neighbours are equal.
teaching_notes: One idea: at a crossing, neighbouring angles add to a straight line and facing angles are equal. Watch for students who think angles side by side must be equal.

source: Ruhee draws two lines that cross and measures the four angles with a protractor
video_script.why: The child sees the pattern among the four angles of a crossing before any rule is named.
video_script.substitution: The four measured angles of the book's activity: two lines are drawn on a plain sheet and the angles are measured with a protractor.
video_script.anchor: Two lines crossing at a point, with the four angles named a, b, c and d going round the crossing.
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko thinks angles that sit side by side must be equal.
video_script.payoff_line: Neighbouring angles add to one hundred and eighty degrees, and facing angles are equal.

final_answer.value: neighbours add to 180°, facing angles are equal, two lines meet at one point only
final_answer.spoken: neighbouring angles add to one hundred and eighty degrees, facing angles are equal, and two straight lines meet at one point only

names.Ruhee: the child who draws two crossing lines and measures the four angles

hold_back: neighbours add to 180°, facing angles are equal
maths_rules: two straight lines meet at one point only, so there are exactly four angles
video_script.design: One crossing stays on the stage all video. The measured angles are written round it; the neighbouring sums and the facing pairs are drawn in two colours.

beats.on_screen: the small title card From your book appears; two lines cross; the four angles a, b, c and d are written round the crossing as 63°, 117°, 63° and 117°

marks.m1: the small title card From your book appears and two lines cross
marks.m2: the four measured angles are written round the crossing
marks.m3: a question mark appears in the anchor band

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>This is a question from your book about Ruhee and two lines that cross.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Ruhee measures the four angles with a protractor.
Going round, they are sixty three, one hundred and seventeen, sixty three and one hundred and seventeen degrees.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>What pattern do the four angles show?

beats.on_screen: the question stays on the board

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board as the child

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.

beats.on_screen: the two lines glow; the crossing point is marked; the four angles are named a, b, c and d going round; one angle is shown with its two neighbours and the one facing it

marks.m1: the two lines glow and the crossing point is marked
marks.m2: the four angles are named a, b, c and d going round
marks.m3: one angle is shown with its two neighbours and the one facing it

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Two lines that meet at a point are called intersecting lines.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>They form four angles at the crossing. Call them eigh, b, c and d going round.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Each angle has two neighbours beside it, and one angle facing it.

marks.m1: the four measured angles are written in the working band

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Given, the four angles going round the crossing are measured.
They are sixty three, one hundred and seventeen, sixty three and one hundred and seventeen degrees.

beats.on_screen: To find: the pattern among a, b, c and d

marks.m1: the words to find are written under the given

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>We have to find the pattern among the four angles.

beats.on_screen: Step 1: add the neighbours. a + b = 63 + 117 = 180; b + c = 117 + 63 = 180

marks.m1: the neighbouring pair a and b lights up with its sum
marks.m2: the neighbouring pair b and c lights up with its sum

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step one, add each pair of neighbours. Sixty three plus one hundred and seventeen gives one hundred and eighty.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>One hundred and seventeen plus sixty three also gives one hundred and eighty.

beats.on_screen: Step 2: compare the facing angles. a = 63° and c = 63°; b = 117° and d = 117°

marks.m1: the facing pairs light up in two colours
marks.m2: the pair a and c is shown equal, then the pair b and d

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step two, compare each angle with the angle facing it.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>The angles eigh and c are both sixty three degrees. The angles b and d are both one hundred and seventeen degrees.

beats.on_screen: Step 3: two straight lines meet at one point only, so there are exactly four angles

marks.m1: the single crossing point is circled and the four angles are counted

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step three, count the meeting points. Two straight lines cannot meet at more than one point, so a crossing always gives exactly four angles.

beats.on_screen: Answer: neighbours add to 180°, facing angles are equal, two lines meet at one point only

marks.m1: the pattern is written and boxed
marks.m2: the single crossing point lights up again

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Neighbouring angles add to one hundred and eighty degrees, and facing angles are equal.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Two straight lines meet at one point only.

beats.on_screen: Keeko with a raised hand beside the crossing
narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Keeko has raised a hand. Let us check the doubt and solve it.

beats.on_screen: Keeko's bubble says neighbours are equal; the neighbours 63° and 117° are shown side by side and the claim is struck out

marks.m1: the bubble with the wrong idea appears
marks.m2: the neighbours 63° and 117° are shown side by side
marks.m3: the claim is struck out and the straight line is drawn in

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Keeko thinks neighbouring angles are equal, because they sit side by side.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>But the neighbour of sixty three degrees is one hundred and seventeen degrees.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Those two are not equal. Neighbours share a straight line, so they add to one hundred and eighty.
